prompt: What happens to a PaaS service's public IP when you configure a service endpoint for it?
choices: It keeps its public IP, restricted to the subnet
It receives an additional private IP alongside the public one
The public IP is removed and replaced by a private one
It becomes reachable only through a VPN Gateway
correctAnswers: It keeps its public IP, restricted to the subnet
explanation: A service endpoint extends your VNet identity over the backbone; the service keeps its public IP but access can be limited to allowed subnets.

prompt: What does a private endpoint give a PaaS service?
choices: A private IP in your VNet, via a dedicated NIC
A restriction of its existing public IP to your own subnet
An encrypted tunnel from the service to on-premises
A faster, dedicated public IP address
correctAnswers: A private IP in your VNet, via a dedicated NIC
explanation: A private endpoint assigns the service a private IP on a NIC inside your VNet, so the public endpoint can be removed entirely. Restricting the public IP to your subnet is the tempting near-answer, however that describes a service endpoint — the address stays public and publicly resolvable.

prompt: Which requirement is unique to private endpoints (and not to service endpoints) for name resolution to work correctly?
choices: Integrating a Private DNS zone for the name
Adding the Storage service tag to the subnet NSG rules
Assigning a managed identity to the client
Enabling a VPN Gateway on the VNet
correctAnswers: Integrating a Private DNS zone for the name
explanation: Private DNS zone integration is unique to private endpoints: without it the service hostname still resolves to its public IP and the private path is never used. The Storage service tag is the tempting alternative because it also names the service, whereas a tag governs NSG rules rather than name resolution.

prompt: A PaaS service must have NO public exposure and be reachable from peered VNets and on-premises over ExpressRoute. Which option meets this?
choices: A private endpoint with public network access disabled
A service endpoint restricting the public IP to your subnet
An NSG rule allowing only the on-premises IP range
A shared access signature scoped to the service
correctAnswers: A private endpoint with public network access disabled
explanation: Only a private endpoint with public network access disabled removes public exposure while staying reachable across peering, VPN and ExpressRoute. A service endpoint is the closest miss and leaves the public endpoint in place, so the "no public exposure" half of the requirement fails.

prompt: After adding a private endpoint to a storage account, what additional setting ensures it can no longer be reached over the public internet?
choices: Set Public network access to Disabled
Rotate both of the account access keys
Enable blob versioning on the account
Enable soft delete on the containers
correctAnswers: Set Public network access to Disabled
explanation: Adding a private endpoint does not automatically close the public endpoint; you must disable public network access explicitly.

prompt: What is an Azure Private Link service (as opposed to a private endpoint)?
choices: A way to publish YOUR service privately
A way to consume a Microsoft PaaS service privately instead
A managed DNS resolver for private endpoints
A global CDN entry point for the web app
correctAnswers: A way to publish YOUR service privately
explanation: A Private Link service publishes your own load-balanced service so that others can reach it through their own private endpoints. Consuming a Microsoft PaaS service privately is the other half of Private Link and is the private endpoint, which is why these two are so often swapped — provider side whereas consumer side.

prompt: What does VNet integration enable for an Azure App Service or Function app?
choices: Outbound calls from the app into a VNet
Inbound calls into the app restricted to a VNet
Encryption of the app's data at rest
A private IP for the app's public endpoint
correctAnswers: Outbound calls from the app into a VNet
explanation: VNet integration handles outbound calls from the app into a VNet. Securing inbound access is a different mechanism entirely — a private endpoint or access restrictions — whereas expecting VNet integration to do both is the confusion this pair exists to test.

prompt: An App Service must call an on-premises SQL Server over a site-to-site VPN, while keeping its normal public inbound endpoint. What should you configure?
choices: VNet integration, into the VPN-linked VNet
A private endpoint on the App Service, for inbound
A service endpoint on the App Service subnet
An App Service Environment instead
correctAnswers: VNet integration, into the VPN-linked VNet
explanation: VNet integration connects the app outbound into the VPN-linked VNet, which is what lets it reach on-premises SQL Server. A private endpoint on the App Service is the tempting answer and points the wrong way: it governs inbound traffic to the app rather than the app's outbound calls.

prompt: Which App Service networking feature secures INBOUND access to the app?
choices: A private endpoint, or access restrictions
A service endpoint on the outbound subnet only
VNet integration on the app subnet
A hybrid connection to on-premises
correctAnswers: A private endpoint, or access restrictions
explanation: Inbound protection for App Service comes from a private endpoint or from access restrictions. VNet integration is the closest miss because it is the other networking feature on the same blade, whereas it only governs the outbound direction.

prompt: What is an App Service Environment (ASE)?
choices: A single-tenant deployment inside your VNet
A shared multi-tenant plan with a private endpoint attached
A staging slot for App Service deployments
A managed DNS zone for App Service apps
correctAnswers: A single-tenant deployment inside your VNet
explanation: An App Service Environment is a single-tenant, fully isolated deployment inside your own VNet, at higher cost and management overhead. It is not multi-tenant App Service with a private endpoint bolted on, which is the cheaper architecture people mistake it for.

prompt: When is an ASE the right choice over multi-tenant App Service with VNet integration and a private endpoint?
choices: When a hard requirement mandates full single-tenant isolation
When you want the lowest cost and least management
When the app is a simple public website with no isolation needs
When you only need outbound access to a VNet
correctAnswers: When a hard requirement mandates full single-tenant isolation
explanation: An ASE is justified when a hard requirement mandates full single-tenant isolation, and by little else. Choosing it for lower cost or simpler management is the inversion to avoid, whereas it is in fact more expensive and more work than multi-tenant App Service with private endpoints.

prompt: How is Azure SQL Managed Instance deployed at the network level?
choices: Into a delegated subnet you secure yourself
Always with a public endpoint and no controls
Only inside an App Service Environment
Only reachable through Azure Bastion hosts
correctAnswers: Into a delegated subnet you secure yourself
explanation: SQL Managed Instance always lands in a delegated subnet that you secure with NSGs and route tables, and a private endpoint can be added on top. Believing it comes with a public endpoint and no controls is the misconception — the subnet delegation is not optional.

prompt: Between service endpoints and private endpoints, which keeps the service's public IP address?
choices: The service endpoint
Neither uses IP addressing
Both remove the public IP
The private endpoint
correctAnswers: The service endpoint
explanation: A service endpoint keeps the service's public IP and restricts which subnets may use it, whereas a private endpoint assigns a private IP inside your VNet. Answering "both remove the public IP" is the belief that leads teams to claim no public exposure when the endpoint is still publicly resolvable.

prompt: A team enabled a service endpoint for Storage but the account is still reachable from other Azure tenants' subnets. Why?
choices: The storage firewall must also allow only your subnet
Service endpoints require public network access to be disabled first
The account needs a private endpoint before any restriction applies
Service endpoints only work with a private DNS zone
correctAnswers: The storage firewall must also allow only your subnet
explanation: The service endpoint marks traffic with your subnet identity, but you still configure the storage account firewall to allow only that subnet and deny others.

prompt: Which sub-resource would you select when creating a private endpoint for a storage account that serves blob data?
choices: blob (for blob data)
sqlServer (for a database)
registry (for images)
vault (for secrets)
correctAnswers: blob (for blob data)
explanation: Private endpoints are created per sub-resource, and for blob data the target group is blob. The other options are sub-resource names of different services — vault for Key Vault, sqlServer for SQL, registry for ACR — whereas picking from the list without checking the service is a real error mode.

prompt: From on-premises over ExpressRoute private peering, a client resolves a storage account name to its PUBLIC IP even though a private endpoint exists. What is the fix?
choices: Conditionally forward DNS to the Azure zone
Enable a service endpoint in addition to the private endpoint
Add the storage service tag to the on-premises firewall
Recreate the private endpoint with a public IP
correctAnswers: Conditionally forward DNS to the Azure zone
explanation: On-premises resolvers must be pointed at (or forward to) the Private DNS zone so the name resolves to the private endpoint IP rather than the public one.

prompt: Which statement about a Private Link service versus a private endpoint is correct?
choices: The provider publishes; the consumer connects
A private endpoint needs a Standard Load Balancer
A Private Link service consumes a PaaS service privately
They are two names for the same single object
correctAnswers: The provider publishes; the consumer connects
explanation: The provider stands up a Private Link service behind a Standard Load Balancer, and each consumer connects with their own private endpoint. Treating them as two names for one object is the trap: they are the two ends of the same connection, configured by different parties.

prompt: Which two networking directions do VNet integration and a private endpoint respectively cover for App Service?
choices: Integration outbound; private endpoint inbound
Integration inbound; private endpoint outbound instead
Both of them cover the outbound direction only
Both of them cover the inbound direction only
correctAnswers: Integration outbound; private endpoint inbound
explanation: They cover opposite directions — VNet integration outbound, whereas a private endpoint is inbound — which is why they are frequently deployed together. Reading either as covering both leaves one direction wide open while the design looks complete.

prompt: You want a Key Vault to be reachable only from within a specific VNet, with no public endpoint at all. Which is the most robust option?
choices: A private endpoint, public access disabled
A service endpoint plus the vault firewall rule
A Conditional Access policy on the vault
An NSG rule on the vault's delegated subnet
correctAnswers: A private endpoint, public access disabled
explanation: A private endpoint removes public exposure entirely; a service endpoint still leaves the vault's public endpoint reachable (restricted). NSGs/Conditional Access don't gate the vault's public endpoint this way.

prompt: Which is a genuine advantage of a private endpoint over a service endpoint?
choices: It works across peering and on-premises
It automatically encrypts the data at rest in the service too
It is free, whereas service endpoints are billed per hour
It requires no DNS configuration at all
correctAnswers: It works across peering and on-premises
explanation: Private endpoints extend privately across peered/on-prem networks and remove public exposure. They do require Private DNS configuration and are not free.

prompt: A serverless Function app needs to reach a database that only accepts traffic from within a VNet. Which feature should you enable on the Function app?
choices: VNet integration on the app
A service endpoint on the database only
A private endpoint on the Function app
Azure Bastion for the app
correctAnswers: VNet integration on the app
explanation: The Function app makes an outbound call into the VNet, which is VNet integration's role. A private endpoint on the app would address inbound access instead.

prompt: Which of these is NOT a valid way to reduce public exposure of an Azure SQL Database (logical server)?
choices: Assigning it a system-assigned identity
Restricting the server firewall to IPs or VNets
Disabling public network access on it
Adding a private endpoint to the server
correctAnswers: Assigning it a system-assigned identity
explanation: A managed identity is about how the server authenticates outbound (e.g. to Key Vault), not about restricting inbound network exposure. The other three all reduce public reachability.

prompt: Why is Azure SQL Managed Instance considered network-isolated by design?
choices: It always lands in a delegated subnet
It runs inside a mandatory App Service Environment instead
It is always assigned a private endpoint automatically
It can only be reached through Azure Bastion
correctAnswers: It always lands in a delegated subnet
explanation: SQL Managed Instance is always deployed into a delegated subnet you control with NSGs and route tables, so it is never on a shared multi-tenant network. It is not assigned a private endpoint automatically, which is the over-reading — the isolation comes from the subnet rather than from Private Link.

prompt: A private endpoint is created but clients inside the VNet still connect to the service's public IP. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The Private DNS zone was never linked
The private endpoint needs a public IP assigned to it
Public network access must be re-enabled
The subnet is missing a service endpoint
correctAnswers: The Private DNS zone was never linked
explanation: Without the Private DNS zone linked to the VNet, clients resolve the public IP and never use the private endpoint at all. Re-enabling public network access is the tempting "fix" because connectivity returns, whereas it confirms the traffic is taking exactly the path you meant to remove.

prompt: Which two options keep traffic to a PaaS service off the public internet? (Choose two.)
choices: Service endpoints on the subnet
Private endpoints in the VNet
Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on the subnet NSG
Disabling TLS on the service
correctAnswers: Service endpoints on the subnet
Private endpoints in the VNet
explanation: Service endpoints and private endpoints both keep PaaS traffic on the Azure backbone rather than the public internet. Allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on the NSG and disabling TLS are tempting only as distractors that sound network-related — both increase exposure rather than reducing it.

prompt: Which two statements about service endpoints are correct? (Choose two.)
choices: The PaaS service keeps a public IP address
Traffic travels over the Azure backbone
The service is assigned a private IP inside the VNet
A Private DNS zone is mandatory for them to function
correctAnswers: The PaaS service keeps a public IP address
Traffic travels over the Azure backbone
explanation: A service endpoint keeps the service's public IP, restricted by subnet, and routes over the Azure backbone. Neither distractor holds: no private IP is assigned inside the VNet, and no Private DNS zone is needed — those are private-endpoint properties.

prompt: Which two reasons justify an App Service Environment over multi-tenant App Service? (Choose two.)
choices: A regulatory single-tenant isolation requirement
A need for a dedicated, isolated deployment
A wish to minimize cost and management overhead
A simple public marketing site with no isolation need
correctAnswers: A regulatory single-tenant isolation requirement
A need for a dedicated, isolated deployment
explanation: An ASE is justified by a regulatory single-tenant isolation requirement or a need for a dedicated isolated deployment. Cost minimisation and a simple public site are the inversions, whereas an ASE is the more expensive and more operationally demanding option.

prompt: Referring to requirement 3 (a backups storage account reachable only from an on-premises network over ExpressRoute, zero public exposure), which configuration is correct?
choices: A private endpoint, public access disabled
A service endpoint restricting the public IP
The storage firewall allowing the on-prem IP
A SAS token issued to the on-premises app
correctAnswers: A private endpoint, public access disabled
explanation: Only a private endpoint with public network access disabled removes all public exposure while remaining reachable from on-premises. The storage firewall allowing the on-premises public IP is the tempting alternative and it keeps the endpoint public, merely narrowing who may use it.

prompt: Referring to requirement 4 (App Service must make outbound calls to on-premises SQL over a site-to-site VPN, keeping its public inbound endpoint), what should be configured?
choices: VNet integration to the VPN-linked VNet
A service endpoint for SQL on the App Service subnet
A private endpoint on the App Service
An App Service Environment instead
correctAnswers: VNet integration to the VPN-linked VNet
explanation: VNet integration into the VPN-linked VNet gives the app outbound reach to on-premises without touching its inbound surface. A private endpoint on the App Service is the closest miss and solves the opposite direction, so the outbound call still fails.

prompt: After deploying the private endpoint for the backups storage account, on-premises clients still resolve its public name. What must Fabrikam fix?
choices: Point on-premises DNS at the Azure zone
Disable the private endpoint, use a service endpoint
Add the Storage service tag to the firewall
Enable public network access on the account
correctAnswers: Point on-premises DNS at the Azure zone
explanation: On-premises resolvers must conditionally forward the storage FQDN to the Azure Private DNS zone, or the name resolves to the public IP from outside Azure. Re-enabling public access is the tempting workaround, whereas it undoes the isolation the private endpoint was deployed for.

prompt: Order the steps to give a storage account a private endpoint with no public exposure.
reorderItems: Create a private endpoint targeting the storage account's 'blob' sub-resource
Integrate the endpoint with a Private DNS zone
Verify the storage account's hostname resolves to the private IP from within the VNet
Set Public network access to Disabled
explanation: The endpoint and its DNS integration must exist and be verified before public access is cut off, otherwise clients lose connectivity with no working path in place. Disabling public access first is the ordering mistake, and it is the one that causes an outage rather than a warning.

prompt: Order the steps to let an App Service reach an on-premises database over a site-to-site VPN while keeping its public inbound endpoint.
reorderItems: Establish a site-to-site VPN connecting the VNet to on-premises
Enable VNet integration on the App Service, pointing to that VNet
Confirm outbound calls from the app reach the on-premises database
Leave the app's default public inbound endpoint unchanged
explanation: The VPN must exist before VNet integration can route through it, with verification following; the app's public endpoint is untouched throughout. Expecting VNet integration to change inbound exposure is the misconception — it never does.

prompt: Configure this simplified private endpoint screen for a Key Vault that must have zero public exposure.
explanation: Key Vault's private endpoint sub-resource is vault, and DNS integration is what lets clients resolve the name to the private IP. Skipping the DNS step is the trap in this screen: the endpoint exists and traffic still goes out over the public endpoint.

prompt: Proposed solution: Rely on SQL Managed Instance's default deployment into a delegated subnet secured with NSGs, with ExpressRoute private peering to on-premises. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: Yes
explanation: SQL MI is never placed on a public multi-tenant network — its delegated-subnet deployment plus ExpressRoute private peering satisfies both reachability and no public exposure.

prompt: Proposed solution: Enable a public endpoint on the SQL Managed Instance and restrict it with a firewall rule allowing only the on-premises public IP. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: This still exposes a public endpoint to the internet, even if restricted by IP — it does not meet 'never exposed to the public internet'.

prompt: Proposed solution: Configure a service endpoint for SQL on the on-premises router. Does this solution meet the goal?
choices: Yes
No
correctAnswers: No
explanation: Service endpoints extend a VNet's identity to a service over the Azure backbone — they don't apply to on-premises routers, so this misapplies the concept entirely.

prompt: Complete the command that creates a private endpoint for the blob service of a storage account.
template: az network private-endpoint create --name PE1 --resource-group RG1 --vnet-name VNet1 --subnet Subnet1 --connection-name conn1 --private-connection-resource-id [[b1]] --group-id [[b2]]
explanation: The connection resource ID names the service being reached, so it is the storage account — not the VNet or subnet, which are already given by their own parameters. The group ID is the SUB-RESOURCE, and every service has its own set: blob, file, table and queue for storage, vault for Key Vault, sqlServer for SQL, registry for ACR. Picking a name from the wrong service is a real error mode, and it fails at creation rather than silently.

prompt: A private endpoint now serves the storage account. Complete the command that removes ALL public reachability from it — not merely narrowing who may use the public endpoint.
template: az storage account update --name stg1 --resource-group RG1 [[b1]] [[b2]]
explanation: `--public-network-access Disabled` removes the public endpoint outright, leaving the private endpoint as the only path in. `--default-action Deny` is the trap and is a perfectly valid pairing that does something weaker: the public endpoint stays up and answers, and only the allow-list decides who gets through. `--allow-blob-public-access false` is narrower still and concerns anonymous container access rather than network reachability.

prompt: Build the sequence that makes the storage account's blob hostname resolve to its private IP from inside VNet1. Not every action in the pool belongs in the answer.
poolItems: Create a private DNS zone whose name matches the service exactly: privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
Link that zone to VNet1 so the VNet resolves against it
Attach the private endpoint to the zone with a DNS zone group, which creates and maintains the A record
Create a public DNS zone named blob.core.windows.net and add the A record by hand
Set VNet1's custom DNS servers to 168.63.129.16
Re-enable public network access on the storage account so the hostname resolves again
Add a Storage service tag rule to the subnet's network security group
correctOrder: Create a private DNS zone whose name matches the service exactly: privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
Link that zone to VNet1 so the VNet resolves against it
Attach the private endpoint to the zone with a DNS zone group, which creates and maintains the A record
explanation: A private endpoint gives the service a private IP, but the public hostname still resolves publicly until DNS is redirected — so all three steps are needed and the zone must be named privatelink.blob.core.windows.net exactly. The distractors are the four ways teams get this wrong: hand-authoring a public zone works until the IP changes, pointing the VNet at 168.63.129.16 changes nothing because that is already the default resolver, re-enabling public access makes connectivity return by undoing the isolation, and a service tag governs NSG rules rather than name resolution.

prompt: Which command enables a SERVICE endpoint for Azure Storage on a subnet — the service keeping a restricted public IP?
choices: az network vnet subnet update
az network private-endpoint create
az network nsg rule create
az storage account update
correctAnswers: az network vnet subnet update
explanation: A service endpoint is a property of the subnet, enabled with `--service-endpoints Microsoft.Storage` when updating it. `az network private-endpoint create` is the closest miss and is the other mechanism entirely: it places a NIC with a private IP in the subnet, whereas a service endpoint leaves the service on its public address and merely restricts which subnets may reach it.

prompt: What distinguishes `--default-action Deny` from `--public-network-access Disabled` on a storage account?
choices: Deny keeps the endpoint; Disabled removes it
Deny applies to blobs only; Disabled to all
Disabled only blocks HTTP, and Deny blocks HTTPS too
They are strictly equivalent in every way
correctAnswers: Deny keeps the endpoint; Disabled removes it
explanation: Default-action Deny keeps the public endpoint and allows only configured exceptions, whereas public-network-access Disabled removes the public endpoint outright. Treating them as equivalent is the trap, since the first still answers on a public address.
